items.title: Lambdas & functional interfaces
items.context: A lambda expression is an anonymous function: (params) -> expression. It's typically used to implement a functional interface — an interface with exactly one abstract method (optionally marked @FunctionalInterface).

questions.prompt: How many abstract methods does a functional interface have?
questions.explanation: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (it may still have default/static methods), which is what a lambda expression implements.

questions.prompt: What best describes a lambda expression?
choices: A named class implementing multiple interfaces
A new primitive data type introduced in Java 8
An anonymous function that can be passed around or stored in a variable
questions.explanation: Lambdas are a concise syntax for an anonymous function, most often used to implement a functional interface inline.

items.title: Stream API: map, filter, reduce
items.context: Streams process collections declaratively without mutating the source. map() transforms each element, filter() keeps elements matching a predicate, and reduce() combines all elements into a single value.

questions.prompt: Which stream operation keeps only elements that satisfy a given condition?
questions.explanation: filter() takes a Predicate and produces a stream containing only the elements for which it returns true.

questions.prompt: In a stream pipeline like stream().filter(...).map(...).toList(), what determines how many elements reach the map() step?
choices: filter() runs after map(), so it has no effect on map()'s input
Only the elements that passed filter()'s predicate reach map()
map() always processes every original element regardless of filter()
The pipeline processes all operations in parallel with no defined order
questions.explanation: Stream operations run in the declared sequence per element: filter() only lets through elements matching its predicate, and only those reach the next operation, like map().

items.title: Optional
items.context: Optional<T> wraps a value that may or may not be present, forcing callers to explicitly consider the absent case instead of risking a NullPointerException.

questions.prompt: What problem is Optional primarily designed to address?
choices: Explicitly signaling and handling a possibly-absent value instead of returning null
questions.explanation: Optional makes 'this might not have a value' part of the type signature, encouraging callers to handle absence explicitly rather than risking a NullPointerException.

questions.prompt: Which Optional method returns a default value when the Optional is empty?
questions.explanation: orElse(default) returns the contained value if present, or the given default otherwise — get() throws if the value is absent, which is exactly what Optional tries to help you avoid calling blindly.

items.title: Predicate vs Function
items.context: Predicate<T> represents a boolean-valued test via test(T) — used for filtering. Function<T,R> represents a transformation via apply(T) that returns an R — used for mapping.

questions.prompt: Which functional interface's abstract method returns a boolean?
questions.explanation: Predicate<T>.test(T) returns a boolean, which is exactly what filter() needs.

items.title: Method references
items.context: Method references are shorthand for a lambda that just calls an existing method: ClassName::staticMethod, object::instanceMethod, or ClassName::new for a constructor.

questions.prompt: Which syntax is a method reference to a static method?
questions.explanation: ClassName::staticMethod (e.g. Integer::parseInt) refers to a static method, usable wherever a matching functional interface is expected.

questions.prompt: Which syntax is a method reference to a constructor?
questions.explanation: ClassName::new refers to a constructor, commonly used as a Supplier<ClassName> or Function<Arg, ClassName> depending on which constructor matches.

items.title: Date and Time API
items.context: Java 8 replaced the old, mutable and not-thread-safe java.util.Date/Calendar with the java.time package: immutable, thread-safe types like LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and Instant.

questions.prompt: Which package did Java 8 introduce with immutable, thread-safe date/time classes like LocalDate?
questions.explanation: java.time (the 'new' Date and Time API) replaced the old, mutable and thread-unsafe java.util.Date/Calendar classes with immutable types like LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and Instant.

items.title: Collectors & collect()
items.context: collect() is a terminal operation that gathers stream elements into a result container using a Collector. Collectors.toList()/toSet() build simple collections; Collectors.groupingBy() partitions elements into groups keyed by a classifier function.

questions.prompt: Which terminal stream operation gathers elements into a List, Set, or Map using a Collector?
questions.explanation: collect() is the general-purpose terminal operation for reducing a stream into a container, driven by a Collector such as Collectors.toList() or Collectors.groupingBy().

questions.prompt: What does Collectors.groupingBy(classifier) produce?
choices: A Map grouping stream elements by the result of the classifier function
questions.explanation: groupingBy() returns a Map<K, List<T>> (by default) where each key is a distinct classifier result and its value is the list of elements that produced that key.

items.title: distinct, sorted & limit
items.context: distinct() removes duplicate elements (based on equals()). sorted() orders elements by natural ordering or a supplied Comparator. limit(n) truncates the stream to at most n elements.

questions.prompt: Which stream operation removes duplicate elements based on equals()?
questions.explanation: distinct() filters out elements that are equal (per equals()) to one already seen earlier in the stream.

questions.prompt: Which stream operation restricts the stream to at most n elements?
questions.explanation: limit(n) truncates the stream so no more than n elements flow through to later operations, useful for pagination-style processing.

items.title: Parallel streams
items.context: Calling parallelStream() (or .parallel() on an existing stream) splits the work across multiple threads using the common ForkJoinPool. It can help with large, CPU-bound, stateless, order-independent workloads, but adds overhead that can hurt performance on small collections or operations with shared mutable state.

questions.prompt: How do you obtain a parallel stream from a collection?
choices: collection.parallelStream(), or .parallel() on an existing stream
Streams are always parallel by default
questions.explanation: Collection.parallelStream() creates a parallel stream directly, and any sequential stream can be converted with .parallel().

questions.prompt: You have a list of only 20 elements and a simple stateless transformation. Is a parallel stream a good idea here?
choices: Only if running on a single-core machine
Usually not — the overhead of splitting work across threads can outweigh the benefit for small, cheap workloads
questions.explanation: Parallel streams add coordination overhead (splitting, thread hand-off, merging); for small collections or cheap per-element work, a sequential stream is often just as fast or faster.

items.title: Default & static methods in interfaces
items.context: Before Java 8, interfaces could only declare abstract methods. Java 8 added default methods (with a body, usable as-is or overridden by implementers) and static methods, letting interfaces evolve without breaking every existing implementation.

questions.prompt: Before Java 8, could an interface method have a method body?
choices: Only in abstract classes, never interfaces
No — interface methods were implicitly abstract until Java 8 added default and static methods
questions.explanation: Prior to Java 8, every interface method was implicitly abstract (no body). Default and static methods, added in Java 8, were the first to allow a body directly in an interface.

questions.prompt: Why were default methods added to interfaces in Java 8?
choices: To let interfaces gain new methods without breaking classes that already implement them
To remove the need for classes entirely
questions.explanation: Default methods let library designers add new methods to widely-implemented interfaces (like adding forEach() to Iterable) while existing implementations keep compiling, inheriting the default body automatically.

items.title: Supplier & Consumer
items.context: Supplier<T> takes no arguments and returns a value via get() — used for lazy value production. Consumer<T> takes an argument and returns nothing via accept() — used for side effects like printing or saving.

questions.prompt: Which functional interface takes no arguments and produces a value?
questions.explanation: Supplier<T>.get() takes nothing and returns a T — useful for lazily producing a value only when it's actually needed.

questions.prompt: Which functional interface takes an argument and performs a side effect, returning nothing?
questions.explanation: Consumer<T>.accept(T) takes a value and returns void — exactly what forEach() uses to act on each stream element.

items.title: flatMap
items.context: map() transforms each element one-to-one. flatMap() is for when each element itself produces a stream (e.g. a List<List<T>>) — it flattens those nested streams into a single, flat stream of the inner elements.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between map() and flatMap() in the Stream API?
choices: map() transforms each element one-to-one; flatMap() flattens each element's own stream/collection into the outer stream
map() is a terminal operation, flatMap() is intermediate
They are interchangeable in every situation
questions.explanation: map() produces one output per input element. flatMap() expects each input element to itself yield a stream (or collection converted to one) and merges all of those into a single flat stream.

questions.prompt: You have a List<List<Integer>> and want a single flat Stream<Integer> containing every inner value. Which operation gets you there?
questions.explanation: flatMap(list -> list.stream()) converts each inner List<Integer> into its own stream and merges all of them into one flat Stream<Integer>, which plain map() cannot do — map() would leave you with a Stream<Stream<Integer>>.

items.title: Stream laziness
items.context: Intermediate operations (map, filter, sorted, ...) are lazy — calling them just builds up a pipeline description, without processing any elements. Nothing actually runs until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count, ...) is invoked, which then pulls elements through the whole pipeline.

questions.prompt: When you call stream.filter(...).map(...), when does the actual filtering and mapping work happen?
choices: Only when a terminal operation like collect() or forEach() is invoked
Immediately, as soon as filter() and map() are called
Never, unless the stream is stored in a variable
questions.explanation: Intermediate operations are lazily evaluated — they just describe the pipeline. Nothing runs until a terminal operation triggers the whole chain to execute, pulling elements through each step.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a terminal stream operation, as opposed to an intermediate one?
questions.explanation: collect() (like forEach(), reduce(), and count()) is terminal — it consumes the stream and produces a result, triggering execution of every intermediate step queued before it.

items.title: Optional anti-patterns
items.context: Optional was designed primarily as a method return type to signal 'may be absent.' Using it as a field type, constructor parameter, or collection element is generally discouraged — and calling .get() without first checking presence defeats its whole purpose.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call .get() on an empty Optional without checking isPresent() first?
choices: It returns a default value automatically
questions.explanation: Optional.get() throws NoSuchElementException when the Optional is empty — calling it blindly reintroduces exactly the kind of unchecked failure Optional was meant to help you avoid; prefer orElse()/orElseGet()/orElseThrow() or check isPresent()/ifPresent() first.

questions.prompt: Is it generally considered good practice to use Optional as a class field type?
choices: Optional cannot be used as a field type at all
Yes, always prefer Optional fields over nullable ones
Generally no — Optional is intended mainly as a method return type, and Optional fields add overhead without much benefit (and aren't serializable)
questions.explanation: Optional wasn't designed for use as a field type (or serialized data); the common guidance is to reserve it for method return values that communicate 'this might not have a result' to callers.

items.title: Primitive streams
items.context: IntStream, LongStream, and DoubleStream are specialized stream types for primitives, avoiding the overhead of autoboxing every element into an Integer/Long/Double the way a Stream<Integer> would.

questions.prompt: Why do IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream exist as separate types instead of just using Stream<Integer>/Stream<Long>/Stream<Double>?
choices: They are required for parallel streams to work
They avoid the performance overhead of autoboxing every primitive value into its wrapper class
Stream<Integer> is not allowed in Java
questions.explanation: A Stream<Integer> would box every int into an Integer object; IntStream (and friends) operate on raw primitives internally, which is significantly more efficient for numeric-heavy processing.

items.title: Effectively final variables in lambdas
items.context: A lambda (or anonymous class) can only capture local variables that are effectively final — never reassigned after initialization. This is required because the lambda may execute later or on another thread, after the enclosing method has already returned.

questions.prompt: Can a lambda expression capture a local variable that is reassigned after the lambda is defined?
choices: Only if the variable is static
Yes, lambdas can capture any local variable
No — captured local variables must be final or effectively final (never reassigned)
questions.explanation: Java requires captured local variables to be effectively final because the lambda might run after the enclosing method has returned (e.g. on another thread); allowing reassignment would create ambiguity about which value the lambda should see.

items.title: Comparator combinators
items.context: Java 8 added default/static methods to Comparator: Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor) builds one from a key function, and thenComparing(...) chains a secondary comparator to break ties on the first one.

questions.prompt: Which Comparator method lets you build one directly from a key-extracting function, e.g. Comparator.comparing(Person::getLastName)?
questions.explanation: Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor) is a static factory that builds a Comparator from a function pulling out the value to compare by — much more concise than implementing compare() by hand.

questions.prompt: You sort a list of people by last name, but want to break ties using first name. Which method chains that secondary comparison?
questions.explanation: thenComparing() appends a secondary Comparator that's only consulted when the primary one considers two elements equal — exactly the tie-breaking behavior needed here.

items.title: A stream can only be consumed once
items.context: Once a terminal operation has run on a stream, that stream is considered consumed — trying to reuse it (calling another operation on the same stream instance) throws IllegalStateException. You need a fresh stream (e.g. calling .stream() again on the source) to traverse the data a second time.

questions.prompt: What happens if you try to call a second terminal operation on a Stream after already running one to completion?
choices: It automatically caches and replays the elements
It throws IllegalStateException — a stream can only be traversed/consumed once
It silently re-runs from the beginning
questions.explanation: Streams aren't reusable data structures like a List — once a terminal operation has pulled elements through the pipeline, that stream instance is spent; you must obtain a new stream (e.g. list.stream() again) to process the data again.

items.title: Short-circuiting stream operations
items.context: Operations like anyMatch(), findFirst(), and limit() are short-circuiting — they can stop processing as soon as they have enough information (a match found, or the limit reached) instead of examining every remaining element, which matters a lot for large or infinite streams.

questions.prompt: Why can anyMatch() on a large stream sometimes finish almost instantly, without examining every element?
choices: It's a short-circuiting operation — it stops as soon as it finds one matching element, without needing to examine the rest
It processes elements in parallel automatically
It only checks the first element
It caches results from previous calls
questions.explanation: anyMatch() (like findFirst() and limit()) is short-circuiting: as soon as it can determine the final answer (one match found), it stops pulling more elements through the pipeline instead of exhaustively processing everything.

items.title: Collectors.joining and Collectors.toMap
items.context: Collectors.joining(delimiter, prefix, suffix) concatenates a stream of Strings into one, with optional separators. Collectors.toMap(keyFn, valueFn) builds a Map from a stream, but throws IllegalStateException on a duplicate key unless you supply a third, merge-function argument telling it how to resolve the collision.

questions.prompt: What does Collectors.joining(", ") do when collecting a Stream<String>?
choices: Concatenates all the strings into one, separated by ", "
questions.explanation: Collectors.joining(delimiter) is purpose-built for combining a stream of strings into a single delimited String, optionally with a prefix and suffix too.

questions.prompt: What happens if Collectors.toMap(keyFn, valueFn) (with no merge function) encounters two elements that produce the same key?
choices: It throws IllegalStateException, since it doesn't know how to resolve the collision without a merge function
The second value silently overwrites the first
It puts both values into a List under that key automatically
questions.explanation: The two-argument Collectors.toMap() has no way to combine colliding values, so it throws IllegalStateException on a duplicate key — you must supply a third merge-function argument (e.g. (a, b) -> a) to say how to resolve that case.

items.title: reduce() with an identity value
items.context: The two-argument reduce(identity, accumulator) combines all stream elements starting from the identity value — on an empty stream, no combination ever happens and reduce() simply returns the identity unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does stream.reduce(0, (a, b) -> a + b) return when called on an empty stream?
choices: 0 — the identity value, since there are no elements to combine
questions.explanation: The identity value acts as both the starting point and the fallback result when there's nothing to reduce — with zero elements, the accumulator never runs even once, so the identity is returned as-is.

items.title: peek() for debugging
items.context: peek() lets you observe elements as they flow through a stream pipeline (e.g. for logging), without transforming them — it's intended purely for debugging/inspection side effects, not for actually mutating shared state as part of the pipeline's real logic.

questions.prompt: What is peek() in the Stream API primarily intended for?
choices: Observing elements mid-pipeline (e.g. for debugging/logging) without transforming them
Converting the stream to a List
questions.explanation: peek() exists mainly as a debugging aid, letting you inspect each element as it passes through — it's not meant to carry real pipeline logic like map() or filter() do, and (being an intermediate operation) may not even run if no terminal operation needs those elements.

items.title: Creating streams from arrays and values
items.context: Arrays.stream(array) creates a stream from an existing array. Stream.of(a, b, c) creates one directly from a fixed list of values (varargs) — both common starting points besides collection.stream().

questions.prompt: Which method creates a Stream directly from an existing array?
questions.explanation: Arrays.stream(array) is the standard way to turn an existing array into a Stream; Stream.of(...) instead takes a fixed set of values (varargs), which happens to also work for an array of objects but behaves differently for primitive arrays.

items.title: boxed() for primitive streams
items.context: IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream are primitive-specialized streams; calling .boxed() converts them into a regular Stream<Integer>/Stream<Long>/Stream<Double>, which is necessary when you need to use a generic Collector (like collecting into a List<Integer>) that primitive streams don't support directly.

questions.prompt: Why would you call .boxed() on an IntStream before collecting it into a List?
choices: IntStream can't be collected with generic Collectors directly; boxed() converts it to a Stream<Integer> that can
To make the stream run in parallel
questions.explanation: IntStream.collect() works with primitive-specific collector operations, but general-purpose Collectors (like Collectors.toList()) expect a Stream<T> of objects — boxed() bridges the gap by wrapping each int into an Integer.

items.title: Comparator.naturalOrder and reverseOrder
items.context: Comparator.naturalOrder() and Comparator.reverseOrder() are static factory methods providing the common natural (or reverse-natural) orderings, avoiding a hand-written lambda for the most basic sorting case.

questions.prompt: What does Comparator.<String>naturalOrder() give you?
choices: A Comparator that reverses the list
A Comparator that sorts by the elements' natural (Comparable) ordering, without writing a lambda
questions.explanation: naturalOrder() hands you a ready-made Comparator delegating to compareTo(), for whenever you want the default ordering without spelling out (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b) yourself; reverseOrder() gives the inverse.

items.title: Files.lines() returns a lazy Stream
items.context: Files.lines(path) returns a lazily-populated Stream<String> of a file's lines, reading on demand rather than loading the whole file upfront. Because it holds an open file handle underneath, it should be used inside a try-with-resources block so the file gets closed once you're done.

questions.prompt: Why should Files.lines(path) typically be used inside a try-with-resources block?
choices: Streams are AutoCloseable only when reading files
It's purely a style preference with no functional impact
It holds an open file handle internally that needs to be closed once the stream is done being used
It always throws an exception otherwise
questions.explanation: Unlike most streams (which don't hold external resources), the stream returned by Files.lines() keeps the underlying file open while lines are read lazily — wrapping it in try-with-resources ensures that file handle gets released even if an exception interrupts processing.

items.title: Reusing a consumed Stream

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
choices: Prints a, b, c after counting
Throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed
questions.explanation: A Stream is single-use: once a terminal operation like count() runs, the stream is considered consumed and closed. Calling forEach() on it afterward throws IllegalStateException. You'd need to build a fresh stream (e.g. from a Supplier) for each traversal.

items.title: Optional.get() on an empty Optional
items.context:
Optional<String> name = Optional.empty();
System.out.println(name.get());

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: Optional.get() throws NoSuchElementException ("No value present") when called on an empty Optional. It's meant to be guarded with isPresent(), or better, replaced with orElse()/orElseGet()/orElseThrow() so the empty case is handled explicitly.

items.title: Lambda capture of a per-iteration variable

questions.prompt: What does this print?
choices: Compile error: current is not effectively final
questions.explanation: Each loop iteration declares a brand-new `current` variable that is never reassigned after initialization, so it's effectively final and legal to capture in the lambda. Each lambda closes over its own copy, so the output is 0, 1, 2 — contrast this with capturing the loop variable i itself, which wouldn't compile.

items.title: Collectors.toMap with a duplicate key

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
choices: Produces {a=apple, b=banana} — later values overwrite earlier ones
questions.explanation: Collectors.toMap(keyFn, valueFn) throws IllegalStateException ("Duplicate key") the moment two elements map to the same key, unless you supply a third merge-function argument to resolve the collision. "apple" and "avocado" both key to 'a', so this throws rather than silently picking one.

items.title: orElse() eager evaluation trap

questions.prompt: Assuming computeExpensiveDefault() has a visible side effect (like printing), what happens?
choices: Throws an exception because the Optional already has a value
computeExpensiveDefault() never runs, since cached has a value
computeExpensiveDefault() always runs, even though its result is discarded
questions.explanation: orElse(x) always evaluates its argument eagerly, before checking whether the Optional is present — because x is a plain value, not a lambda. If the fallback is expensive or has side effects, use orElseGet(() -> ...) instead, which only runs the supplier when the Optional is actually empty.

items.title: Diamond conflict between two default methods

questions.prompt: What happens when this code is compiled?
choices: Runtime error when name() is first called
Compile error: class C must override name() to resolve the conflict
questions.explanation: When a class inherits two default methods with the same signature from unrelated interfaces, the compiler can't pick a winner for you — it's a compile-time error ("class C inherits unrelated defaults"). C must explicitly override name(), optionally delegating with A.super.name() or B.super.name().

items.title: sorted() on non-Comparable objects

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: sorted() with no arguments uses the elements' natural ordering, which requires them to implement Comparable. Point doesn't, so at runtime the stream tries to cast a Point to Comparable and throws ClassCastException. Fixing it means either implementing Comparable<Point> or calling sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(p -> p.x)).

items.title: Lazy evaluation with an infinite stream

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
choices: Hangs forever trying to build an infinite stream
questions.explanation: Stream.iterate produces an infinite lazy stream — nothing is actually computed until a terminal operation pulls elements through it. limit(5) tells the pipeline to stop pulling after 5 elements, so only 5 values are ever generated. Streams are lazy by design, which is exactly what makes infinite streams usable.

items.title: map() vs flatMap()

questions.prompt: What does this print, and how would you get a flat list of 4 ints instead?
choices: 4 — this already produces a flat list
2 — map() keeps the nested structure; flatMap() is needed to flatten it
questions.explanation: map() applies a 1-to-1 transformation, so mapping each inner List to itself keeps a Stream<List<Integer>> with 2 elements. To get a flat Stream<Integer> of all 4 numbers you need flatMap(List::stream), which replaces each element with a stream of its own and merges them into one stream.

items.title: Class method overriding an interface default

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Java's resolution rule is simple here: a class's own method always wins over an inherited interface default method, no override annotation required to make it take effect. Default methods only matter when the implementing class doesn't provide its own version.
